```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

mortensor builds probabilistic mortality forecasts from data observed at
different granularities. A forecast is assembled from interchangeable parts:

1. **data** in their original resolution (`mt_data()`), prepared with
   general steps: subsets of ages, years and strata (`mt_subset()`),
   aggregation layers such as deprivation quintiles or cause groups
   (`mt_group_levels()`), exposures from populations (`mt_as_exposure()`),
2. **harmonisation** onto a modelling grid (`mt_ungroup()`, `mt_smooth()`,
   `mt_regroup()`), bundled as a preprocessing pipeline (`mt_prep()`),
3. a **model** (`lee_carter()`, `li_lee()`, `rwd()`, `tucker3()`,
   `apc_bayes()`, ...), fitted with `mt_fit()` and forecast with
   `mt_forecast()` as simulated paths,
4. **derived quantities** computed path by path (`life_expectancy()`,
   `prob_dying()`, `asr()`), and
5. **evaluation** with rolling-origin backtests (`mt_backtest()`,
   `mt_score()`).

This vignette forecasts mortality in England by sex and deprivation.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
```

## Data

`ons_data` holds death registrations and mid-year populations by sex,
5-year age group and decile of the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD),
England 2001-2019, from an ONS ad hoc release (Source: Office for National
Statistics licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0). Decile 1 is the
most deprived.

```{r}
head(ons_data[, 1:8])
```

`mt_data()` reads tables in long format, one row per cell: here the
all-cause deaths and the mid-year populations, with sex and IMD decile as
stratum variables (`by`). Age groups such as `"<1"`, `"01-04"` and `"90+"`
are recognised. `mt_as_exposure()` takes the mid-year population as the
person-years at risk:

```{r}
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
```

Deciles are combined to quintiles with `mt_group_levels()`, which adds an
aggregation layer to any stratum variable (cause groups, regions,
deprivation): deaths and exposures of deciles 1 and 2 are summed to quintile
1, and so on. A function maps the deciles to the quintiles, and `name`
labels the new layer:

```{r}
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
x
mt_strata(x)
```

The deciles are defined by the IMD version current at the time of
registration, so areas move between deciles four times in this period
(column `imd_version` of `ons_data`: 2004, 2007, 2010, 2015 and 2019).

`mt_validate()` checks plausibility (deaths without exposure, rates above
1, gaps in the grid, and the sums of aggregate strata):

```{r}
mt_validate(x)
```

Observed life expectancy at birth shows the deprivation gradient:

```{r}
m <- mt_array(x, "deaths") / mt_array(x, "exposure")
e0 <- life_expectancy(m, mt_grid(x)$age)
round(e0[c("2001", "2010", "2019"), ], 1)
```

## Harmonisation

The data have 5-year age groups (with `<1`, `1-4` and `90+`), and the grid
is set to them, so models can be fitted directly. When single years of age
are needed, `mt_ungroup()` estimates single-year deaths and exposures with
the penalized composite link model; deaths are ungrouped as rates with the
exposures as offset, and the estimates add up to the observed totals.

```{r}
xs <- mt_set_grid(mt_window(x, 2019, 2019), age = single_ages(0, 90))
u <- mt_ungroup(xs)
u
```

The grid keeps the open interval 90+ of the data: splitting it into single
years would rest on its total alone.

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_ungroup(xs, u, period = 2019, strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5"))
```

In a forecasting pipeline, ungrouping is a preprocessing step
(`mt_prep(step_ungroup())`), so that backtests refit it on every training
window. Whether it improves forecasts is a question for the backtest below;
here we model the 5-year groups.

## Fitting and forecasting

`lee_carter()` fits one model per stratum. `li_lee()` adds a common trend:
with `common_by = "sex"` the five quintiles of each sex share one trend, and
their deviations from it follow stationary processes, so the gaps between
quintiles can neither vanish nor explode.

```{r}
fit_lc <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), x)
fit_ll <- mt_fit(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), x)
fc_ll <- mt_forecast(fit_ll, h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
fc_ll
```

The forecast holds 500 simulated paths per age, year and stratum.
`mt_summarise()` returns means and quantiles:

```{r}
s <- mt_summarise(fc_ll)
s[age == "70-74" & period %in% c(2020, 2034) & quintile %in% c("Q1", "Q5"),
  .(sex, quintile, period, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_forecast(fc_ll, ages = c("50-54", "70-74", "85-89"),
                 strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5", "male.Q1", "male.Q5"))
```

## Derived quantities

Life expectancy is computed for every path, so its interval reflects the
joint uncertainty of all ages:

```{r}
e0_fc <- life_expectancy(fc_ll, at = 0)
e0_fc[period %in% c(2020, 2034) & quintile %in% c("Q1", "Q5"), .(sex, quintile, period, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_life_expectancy(fc_ll, at = 65)
```

Because the draws are paths, differences between strata carry their own
uncertainty. The gap in life expectancy at birth between the least (Q5) and
the most deprived quintile (Q1), path by path, for Li-Lee and for separate
Lee-Carter models:

```{r}
st <- mt_strata(x)
gap_paths <- function(fc, model) {
  e <- life_expectancy(fc$rates, fc$age)   # [period, stratum, draw]
  rbindlist(lapply(c("female", "male"), function(sx) {
    g <- e[, st$label == paste0(sx, ".Q5"), ] - e[, st$label == paste0(sx, ".Q1"), ]
    q <- apply(g, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
    data.table(model = model, sex = sx, period = as.numeric(colnames(q)), lo = q[1, ], med = q[2, ], hi = q[3, ])
  }))
}
fc_lc <- mt_forecast(fit_lc, h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
gaps <- rbind(gap_paths(fc_ll, "Li-Lee"), gap_paths(fc_lc, "Lee-Carter"))
gaps[period %in% c(2020, 2034)]
observed_gap <- rbindlist(lapply(c("female", "male"), function(sx) {
  data.table(sex = sx, period = 2001:2019, gap = e0[, paste0(sx, ".Q5")] - e0[, paste0(sx, ".Q1")])
}))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(gaps, aes(period)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = model), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = med, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(data = observed_gap, aes(y = gap)) +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gap in life expectancy at birth, Q5 - Q1 (years)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

The two models make different assumptions, and the data cannot decide
between them. The observed gap was stable for men and widened for women,
with a step in 2013, when the deciles switched to IMD 2015. Separate
Lee-Carter models extrapolate each quintile's own trend, so the female gap
keeps widening, with wide intervals. Li-Lee lets the quintiles deviate from
a common trend only through stationary processes, so gaps return towards
their average of the training years. Its forecasts also start from the
fitted rates of 2019, which for women in Q1 are about 0.4 years of life
expectancy above the observed ones. `li_lee(jump_off = "observed")` removes
this step, but in backtests on these data it forecast worse (CRPS 0.071
against 0.067).

Other quantities work the same way, for example the probability of dying
between ages 40 and 75 and age-standardised rates (European Standard
Population 2013):

```{r}
prob_dying(fc_ll, from = 40, to = 75)[period == 2034 & quintile %in% c("Q1", "Q5"),
                                      .(sex, quintile, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)]
asr(fc_ll)[period == 2034 & quintile %in% c("Q1", "Q5"), .(sex, quintile, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)]
```

## Honest backtests

`mt_backtest()` cuts the data at each forecast origin, refits the
preprocessing and the model on the training window, and scores predictive
draws against the observed deaths. Here the forecasts from origins 2008 to
2014 are scored on 2009 to 2019.

```{r}
origins <- 2008:2014
specs <- list(lee_carter(), li_lee(common_by = "sex"), rwd(),
              ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), rw = rwd()))
bt <- rbindlist(lapply(specs, function(sp) mt_backtest(sp, x, origins = origins, h = 5, n_draws = 200)))
mt_score(bt, by = "model")
```

Lower CRPS and WIS are better; `cov50`, `cov80` and `cov95` are the shares
of observations inside the central 50%, 80% and 95% intervals. Li-Lee is
the most accurate; like Lee-Carter its intervals are too narrow, while the
mixture of Lee-Carter and the random walk is close to nominal coverage at a
small cost in accuracy.

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_scores(bt, by = "horizon")
mt_plot_coverage(bt)
```
